chief_complaint: massive hematemesis of bright red blood and melena stools in cirrhosis patient causing hemodynamic instability
hpi_details: 56M alcoholic cirrhosis patient presenting with active profuse hematemesis and BP 82/50 requiring immediate 2 large-bore IVs, blood resuscitation, IV Octreotide infusion, prophylactic Ceftriaxone, and emergent upper endoscopy for variceal band ligation.
ideas: He thinks one of the enlarged veins in his food pipe that his liver specialist warned him about has finally ruptured and started bleeding.
concerns: He is terrified that he will rapidly bleed to death right here just like a friend from his support group did.
expectations: He hopes the doctor can perform an emergency procedure or give him medicine right away to stop the bleeding.
pmh: Alcoholic cirrhosis with known esophageal varices, hypertension

clinical_knowledge.topic: Acute Upper GI Bleed from Esophageal Varices evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Acute Upper GI Bleed from Esophageal Varices is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes Evidence-based diagnostic and therapeutic protocol for Acute Upper Gastrointestinal Bleed Esophageal Varices, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

Objective/Exam findings: Complete vital signs and focused physical examination required. Diagnostic workup tailored for Acute Upper Gastrointestinal Bleed Esophageal Varices.

common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Acute Upper GI Bleed from Esophageal Varices.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Peptic ulcer bleeding without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Ongoing hematemesis with low blood pressure — active life-threatening hemorrhage.
management_principles: Resuscitate with large-bore IV access and blood products as needed, start vasoactive therapy and antibiotic prophylaxis promptly, and arrange urgent endoscopic variceal ligation after initial stabilization
Refer to specialty team and provide comprehensive patient counseling
Assess clinical stability, monitor vital parameters, and perform targeted diagnostic investigations.
Implement targeted therapeutic interventions per evidence-based clinical practice guidelines.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with symptoms of Acute Upper Gastrointestinal Bleed Esophageal Varices: massive hematemesis of bright red blood and melena stools in cirrhosis patient causing hemodynamic instability. 56M alcoholic cirrhosis patient presenting with active profuse hematemesis and BP 82/50 requiring immediate 2 large-bore IVs, blood resuscitation, IV Octreotide infusion, prophylactic Ceftriaxone, and emergent upper endoscopy for variceal band ligation.
reference_soap.objective: Complete vital signs and focused physical examination required. Diagnostic workup tailored for Acute Upper Gastrointestinal Bleed Esophageal Varices.
reference_soap.assessment: Clinical presentation highly suggestive of Acute Upper Gastrointestinal Bleed Esophageal Varices.
reference_soap.plan: Resuscitate with two large-bore IVs, type and crossmatch, and blood products as needed while protecting the airway if mental status, active hematemesis, or aspiration risk warrants it. Start octreotide and ceftriaxone promptly. Arrange urgent endoscopy after initial hemodynamic stabilization for variceal band ligation; involve GI, critical care, and hepatology. If bleeding is uncontrolled, escalate to balloon tamponade as a bridge and urgent TIPS evaluation.

teaching.diagnosis: Acute Upper GI Bleed from Esophageal Varices
teaching.one_liner: Portal hypertension from cirrhosis causes dilated esophageal veins that can rupture catastrophically, causing massive vomiting of blood and hemodynamic instability — treated with octreotide, antibiotics, and urgent endoscopic band ligation.
red_flags: Ongoing hematemesis with low blood pressure — active life-threatening hemorrhage

must_ask.say: How much blood have you vomited, and what color is it?
Have your stools been black or tarry?
Do you have liver disease, and have you had bleeding like this before?
How much alcohol do you drink?

I vomited pure blood twice in the last two hours, about two large bowls full each time.

No, there was no dry heaving or vomiting regular food beforehand; it just came up as straight blood right away.
Yes, yesterday and earlier this morning I passed two very loose, jet-black, foul-smelling stools like tar.

No, I haven't had burning stomach pain or pain after eating.
No, I did not have any tearing chest pain or back pain after throwing up.
Yes, I was diagnosed with liver cirrhosis from drinking three years ago, and my doctor told me I had swollen veins in my esophagus.
No, this is the very first time I have ever thrown up blood or had variceal bleeding.
My belly has been getting more swollen over the past few months, and my socks leave deep indents on my legs.
Yes, my eyes have looked yellowish for the past few weeks.
Yes, I have noticed large purple bruises on my arms and legs even without bumping into anything.

No, I do not take aspirin, ibuprofen, naproxen, or any blood thinners.

I have liver cirrhosis and high blood pressure, but no diabetes or heart trouble.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 82/50 mmHg, pulse is 118 beats per minute, respiratory rate is 22 breaths per minute, temperature is 36.6°C, and oxygen saturation is 96% on room air.
Patient appears pale, diaphoretic, acutely ill, and weak, with fresh blood stains around his mouth and on his hospital gown.
Marked conjunctival pallor and moderate scleral icterus are present bilaterally.
No blood or bleeding source seen in the nasal cavity or oral mucosa; traces of fresh red blood noted in the oropharynx.
Tachycardic rate with regular rhythm, normal S1 and S2, and no murmurs, rubs, or gallops.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally with no rales, rhonchi, or wheezing.
Multiple spider angiomas on the upper chest and shoulders, palmar erythema on both hands, and scattered ecchymoses on the forearms.
Moderately distended abdomen with visible engorged collateral veins across the abdominal wall.
Abdomen is soft with mild non-localized fullness, no tenderness, and no guarding or rigidity.
Liver edge is firm and irregular, and the spleen tip is palpable 2 cm below the left costal margin.
Positive shifting dullness and a detectable fluid wave consistent with moderate ascites.
Grossly black, tarry, foul-smelling stool coating the glove, with no visible external hemorrhoids.
Bilateral 2+ pitting edema extending up to the mid-shins.
Alert but lethargic, oriented to person and place, responds slowly but coherently to questions.
